SUMMARY 
This report recommends that City Council state its intention to designate the property at 
106 Beverley Street under Part IV, Section 29 of the Ontario Heritage Act for its cultural 
heritage value according to the Statement of Significance which includes a description 
of heritage attributes found in Attachment 1. 
The subject property at 106 Beverley Street, known originally as Esten House (1855), 
and later as Georgina House (1909), is located on the west side of Beverley Street, 
south of Dundas Street West, within the Grange neighbourhood of downtown Toronto. 
A location map and current photograph of the heritage property are included in 
Attachment 2. 
Constructed in 1855 for Toronto lawyer James Esten, the property contains a three-
storey detached house-form building in the Italianate architectural style, which was 
designed by architect James Grand. Following its sale to philanthropist Georgina 
Broughall, who converted the property into an interdenominational women’s residence, 
the renamed Georgina House underwent extensive interior and exterior alterations and 
additions. These modifications were overseen by architect Eden Smith, including 
unspecified interior alterations, the front verandah (1909), a four-storey rear addition 
(1912), and the Osler Wing (1914), which was officially opened via public ceremony by 
His Royal Highness the Duke of Connaught. The property forms part of the historic 
residential context of the Grange neighbourhood, comprising Victorian- and Edwardian-
era houses interspersed with places of worship and institutional buildings. Georgina 
House fits within this context of mid- to late-Victorian era houses and reflects this 
important period of development in Toronto. 
The subject property at 106 Beverley Street was listed on the City of Toronto's Heritage 
Register on November 21, 1977.

STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE 
(REASONS FOR DESIGNATION) 
The property at 106 Beverley Street is worthy of designation under Part IV, Section 29 
of the Ontario Heritage Act for its cultural heritage value and meets Ontario Regulation 
9/06, the provincial criteria prescribed for municipal designation. 
Description 
The subject property at 106 Beverley Street is located on the west side of Beverley 
Street, south of Dundas Street West, within the Grange neighbourhood of downtown 
Toronto. Constructed in 1855, the property contains a three-storey detached house-
form building in the Italianate architectural style designed by architect James Grand, 
which was later known as Georgina House, together with a front verandah and four-
storey residential addition added by architect Eden Smith between 1909 and 1914. The 
property forms part of the historic residential context of the Grange neighbourhood, 
comprising Victorian- and Edwardian-era houses interspersed with places of worship 
and institutional buildings. 
Statement of Cultural Heritage Value 
Design and Physical Value 
The property at 106 Beverley Street has design and physical value as a representative 
example of the Italianate architectural style in the City of Toronto. The Italianate style is 
a classically derived architectural style that was employed for residential and 
commercial architecture across the British colonies and the United States through the 
19th century and could be adapted for urban contexts, as with 106 Beverley Street, as 
well as suburban and rural contexts where it could take on a more picturesque quality. 
The subject property displays the defining characteristics of the Italianate style through 
the symmetrical central mass of its primary (east) façade organized into four bays, its 
brick cladding (painted), and its classical arrangement of elliptical second-storey window 
openings and rectangular third-storey window openings. Characteristic detailing of the 
style visible at 106 Beverley Street includes drip moulds with vermiculated keystones 
over the second-storey windows, brick quoins framing the second storey, a brick string 
course below the third-storey windows, and a large cornice with brackets that returns 
onto the north and south façades. Behind the main house-form building an ‘ell’ extends 
to the rear, more restrained in ornamentation but retaining the brick quoins and window 
openings of the main house. 
Historical and Associative Value 
The property at 106 Beverley Street has historical and associative value through its 
direct associations with a succession of individuals and organizations significant to the 
community. The house was built in 1855 for James Christie Palmer Esten (1805–1864), 
106 Beverley Street - Notice of Intention to Designate Page 6 of 28

a Bermuda-born lawyer who rose to prominence in Toronto’s legal community, was 
appointed Vice-Chancellor in 1849, and, alongside William Blake and John Godfrey 
Spragge, helped establish the prevailing practice of the Court of Chancery, a judicial 
body that later merged with common law courts but was an important institution in 
administering justice on issues pertaining to fairness, equity, trusts, and injunctions. 
From 1871 to 1886, the property was home to John Jacques (1804–1886), the 
cabinetmaker and furniture manufacturer who, with his business partner Robert Hay, is 
credited with introducing high-quality, mass-produced furniture to Southern Ontario 
through the firm Jacques & Hay and with establishing a distinct regional furniture style. 
The property has further historical and associative value through its long association 
with Georgina House and its founder, Georgina Broughall (1843–1928). Broughall, the 
wife of the Reverend Abraham James Broughall of St. Stephen-in-the-Fields Anglican 
Church, recognized a need for secure housing for the increasing number of women 
arriving in Toronto seeking education and employment, and petitioned Anglican 
parishes, the business community, and the public to establish the residence. Georgina 
House opened at 106 Beverley Street in 1909 as an interdenominational women’s 
residence, and through much of the 20th century provided housing and a sense of 
community for women arriving in Toronto from across Canada and internationally, 
regardless of social, cultural, religious, or ethnic background. Run by an all-woman 
board of management from 1917, the organization responded to the needs of an 
exclusively female clientele during a period in which women were achieving economic 
autonomy and making significant gains in equality. 
The property additionally has associative value as it reflects the work of the James 
Grand (1819–1871), an English-born architect who trained with Cumberland & Storm 
before establishing his own Toronto practice and whose commissions included the 
Toronto Exchange Building (1854), the Ontario Veterinary College (1869), and, with 
William G. Storm, the Parliament, Bathurst, and York Street Schools (1871); Georgina 
House is one of Grand's few remaining buildings in Toronto. 
Contextual Value 
The property at 106 Beverley Street has contextual value as it is important in defining, 
maintaining, and supporting the historic character of Beverley Street and the Grange 
neighbourhood. The Grange is a primarily residential district of Victorian- and 
Edwardian-era houses interspersed with places of worship and institutional buildings, 
and Beverley Street and its immediately adjacent streets contain the area’s largest and 
most prestigious homes. Georgina House fits within this context of mid- to late-Victorian 
era houses and reflects this important period of development in Toronto. 
The property also has contextual value as it is physically, visually, and historically linked 
to its surroundings. It stands among a group of the area’s most prestigious residences. 
This includes Boulton’s the Grange (317 Dundas Street West, 1817), George 
Beardmore’s Chudleigh (136 Beverley Street, 1890), John Cawthra’s Devon House 
(150 Beverley Street, 1875), and George Brown’s Lambton Lodge (50 Baldwin Street 
and 186 Beverley Street, 1876). Georgina House is sited directly across from the Art 
Gallery of Ontario and the Grange, with Grange Park extending to the south. Through

its siting and long-standing presence, the subject property is historically and visually 
linked to this established historic residential setting. 
Heritage Attributes 
Design and Physical Value 
Attributes that contribute to the property at 106 Beverley Street being a representative 
example of the Italianate architectural style include: 
• The scale, form and massing of the three-storey detached house-form building, set 
back from Beverley Street 
• The symmetrical four-bay composition of the primary (east) façade 
• The brick cladding 
• The elliptical second-storey window openings and the rectangular third-storey 
window openings on the primary (east) façade 
• The drip moulds with vermiculated keystones and sills over the second-storey 
windows 
• The brick quoins framing the second storey 
• The brick string course below the third-storey windows 
• The wooden cornice with simple brackets, with larger brackets at the corners, 
returning onto the north and south façades 
Historical and Associative Value 
Attributes that contribute to the historical and associative value of the property at 106 
Beverley Street through its associations with James Esten, John Jacques, Georgina 
Broughall, and Georgina House, and with the architect James Grand, include: 
• The 1855 house-form building, designed by the architect James Grand and 
constructed for James Christie Palmer Esten 
• The siting and orientation of the house on the west side of Beverley Street, reflecting 
its mid-19th century construction as one of the larger residences in the area 
• The verandah enclosing the first storey, including its rectangular columns, simple 
roof with cornice, wood railings and spindles, and beamed ceiling, as a prominent, 
public-facing feature of the 1909 Georgina House conversion. 
Contextual Value 
Attributes that contribute to the contextual value of the property at 106 Beverley Street 
as part of the historic residential character of Beverley Street and the Grange 
neighbourhood include: 
• The placement and siting of the building on the west side of Beverley Street, south 
of Dundas Street West 
• The orientation of the primary (east) façade towards Beverley Street 
• The scale and form of the house in relation to the surrounding Victorian- and 
Edwardian-era residences of the Grange neighbourhood

Indigenous Communities 
For time immemorial, Toronto has been home to Indigenous peoples. Ojibway oral 
histories speak of Ice People, who lived at a time when ice covered the land.1 Following 
the retreat of glaciers approximately 13,000 years ago, small groups of Indigenous 
peoples moved from place to place, hunting and gathering the food they needed 
according to the seasons. Over millennia, they adapted to dramatically changing 
environmental conditions, developing and acquiring new technologies as they did 
so. Waterways and the lake were vital sources of fresh water and nourishment, and 
shorelines and nearby areas were important sites for gathering, trading, hunting, fishing, 
and ceremonies. Long-distance trade moved valuable resources across the land. 
After maize and squash were introduced to Southern Ontario, by approximately 500 CE, 
horticulture began to supplement food sources. By 1300 CE, villages focused on 
growing food became year-round settlements surrounded by crops. These villages were 
home to ancestors of the Huron-Wendat Nation, who would continue to occupy 
increasingly larger villages in the Toronto area and beyond. These villages were 
connected to well-established travel routes which were part of local and long-distance 
trail networks, including the Carrying Place trails on the Don, Rouge and Humber rivers 
that connected Lake Ontario to Georgian Bay. Beads made from seashells from the 
eastern seaboard were found at the Alexandra site in North York, which was a 
community of 800-1000 people in approximately 1350. 
By 1600, the Wendat had formed a confederation of individual nations, and had 
concentrated most of their villages away from Lake Ontario, in the Georgian Bay area. 
Following contact with French explorers and missionaries in Southern Ontario in the 
early 1600s, European diseases decimated First Nations. Competition for furs to trade 
with Europeans and the desire to replenish numbers through absorption of captives, 
among other factors2, contributed to the Beaver Wars, which after 1640, saw the 
Haudenosaunee Confederacy expand into Southern Ontario, dispersing the Wendat. 
Within the boundaries of today's Toronto, the Haudenosaunee Confederacy then 
occupied villages on the Carrying Place trails on the Humber and Rouge Rivers from 
approximately the 1660s to the 1680s. 
In the late 1680s, the Haudenosaunee Confederacy chose to leave their village in the 
Toronto area and returned to their homelands in upstate New York. As evidenced by the 
1701 Great Peace of Montreal, the 1701 Nanfan Treaty, and the Dish with One Spoon 
Treaty, the Haudenosaunee continued to have an interest in the resources of the area.

Anishinaabe people from the Lake Superior region then moved into the Toronto area. 
While the Wendat and Haudenosaunee people lived in year-round villages surrounded 
by crops, the Anishinaabe people continued to live primarily by seasonally moving 
across the land to hunt, fish and gather resources that were available at a specific time, 
including migrating birds and maple syrup. To the west of Toronto, the Anishinaabe 
people became known as the Mississaugas of the Credit. To the east, they became 
known as the Chippewas of Beausoleil, Georgina Island and Rama and the 
Mississaugas of Alderville, Curve Lake, Hiawatha, Scugog Island.3 
In 1787, as the British began to prepare for an influx of colonists into the area following 
the American Revolution, the British Crown negotiated the Toronto Purchase with the 
Mississaugas of the Credit First Nation to obtain title to the land. The flawed and poorly 
documented agreement was invalidated, and Treaty 13 was negotiated in 1805 for 
lands now including much of the City of Toronto. In 1923, the Governments of Ontario 
and Canada signed the Williams Treaties for over 20,000 km2, including portions of 
eastern Toronto, with seven First Nations of the Chippewa of Lake Simcoe (Beausoleil, 
Georgina Island and Rama) and the Mississauga of the north shore of Lake Ontario 
(Alderville, Curve Lake, Hiawatha and Scugog Island). 
The Mississaugas, Chippewa, the Haudenosaunee, or the Wendat did not traditionally 
regard land as a commodity to be sold. Following the Toronto Purchase, the British 
government quickly set out to survey the land into lots which were either sold or granted 
into private ownership of settlers. In 2010, the Government of Canada settled the 
Toronto Purchase Claim with the Mississaugas of the Credit after agreeing that the 
Mississaugas were originally unfairly compensated. In 2018, the Williams Treaties First 
Nations settled litigation about land surrenders and harvesting rights with the 
Governments of Canada and Ontario. 
The City of Toronto remains the traditional territory of many nations including the 
Mississaugas of the Credit, the Anishnabeg, the Chippewa, the Haudenosaunee and 
the Wendat peoples and is now home to many diverse First Nations, Inuit and Métis 
peoples. Toronto is also covered by Treaty 13 signed with the Mississaugas of the 
Credit, and the Williams Treaties signed with seven Mississaugas and Chippewa First 
Nations.

The following section outlines the history and facts related to the properties which are 
the basis for determining historical or associative value of Criteria 4, 5 or 6 according to

The Grange Neighbourhood 
The subject property at 106 Beverley Street is located within the former Concession 1 
From the Bay, Park Lot 14. Park Lot 14 was surveyed following the establishment of the 
Town of York in 1793 and was one of the original 32 park lots reserved by Lieutenant-

Governor John Graves Simcoe to entice officials to settle in the town and aid in the 
governance of Upper Canada. 
Park Lot 14 was bound by Lot Street (Queen Street), Huron Street, Beverley Street and 
Bloor Street, and was granted to Peter Russell, a highly influential official with both the 
Executive and Legislative Councils, and the Administrator of Upper Canada following 
Simcoe’s return to England in 1796. Peter Russell’s “Russell Abbey” town house was 
located near the present-day intersection of Princess and Front Street East, with Park 
Lot 14 serving as his farm property which he called “Petersfield.” Peter Russell passed 
away in 1808 after which Park Lot 14 passed to his half-sister Elizabeth Russell, 
followed by Maria Willcocks and Phoebe Baldwin (1822). Phoebe Baldwin’s husband, 
William Baldwin, sold the property to D’Arcy Boulton in 1828 forming part of Boulton’s 
extensive land holdings running south from Spadina House to the Town of York. 
In 1848, Sarah Ann Boulton (wife of D’Arcy Boulton) sold the property to the lawyer, 
politician and investor John Hillyard Cameron and Frances Metcalfe. Cameron had 
recently been appointed to the Executive Council of Upper Canada, in 1846, and had 
financial interests in the Toronto and Guelph Railway, the Canada Life Assurance 
Company and the Toronto and Georgian Bay Canal Company, along with extensive 
land holdings. 
In 1854/55 Hillyard Cameron sold the portion of Park Lot 14 containing 106 Beverley 
Street to James Christie Palmer Esten (1805-1864). Esten had been born in St. 
George’s, Bermuda, the son of the Chief Justice and grandson of the Attorney General 
of the Bermuda Islands. He studied and first practised law in England before 
immigrating to Toronto in 1836/1837.4 Esten arrived in Toronto to establish a career in 
retail merchandising, however with the establishment of the Court of Chancery soon 
after his arrival he renewed his legal practice in equity law. Esten excelled in Toronto’s 
growing legal community; in 1849 he was appointed Vice-Chancellor, and, along with 
William Blake and John Godfrey Spragge, Esten established the Chancery Court’s 
prevailing practice.5 
106 Beverley Street 
In 1854, an advertisement ran in The Globe seeking tenders to construct a dwelling 
house on Beverly (sic) Street for Major Esten to plans and specifications prepared by 
James Grand, Architect, 63 Adelaide Street West. By 1858, James Esten, along with his 
wife and family, are identified as living at the subject property in the City Directories and 
identified as 90 St. George’s Square. By 1860, the property was once again identified 
as Beverley Street (#90). 
Esten resided at 106 Beverley Street until his passing in 1864; in 1866 the property was 
sold by his estate to J. S. McMurray for 1,325 pounds. McMurray was a lawyer and a 
prolific land investor, and in 1871 filed a Plan of Subdivision (Plan D116) which included

John Jacques, along with his wife Mary, lived at 106 Beverley Street through his 
retirement years from 1871 until his passing in 1886; Mary continued to live at the 
subject property until her passing, after which their daughter, Jane Jacques Stewart, 
sold the house in 1902 to the Church Extension Association. 
The Church Extension Association was affiliated with the Anglican Church and 
established in 1864 in England with the intent of establishing schools and orphanages 
for those in need. City Directories from 1902 suggest the intent was to establish a 
school associated with the Church of England, however the following year the property 
once again changed hands having been purchased by Georgina Broughall for $9,000. 
Georgina transferred the property to Georgina Houses Incorporated later that year.7 
In 1909, Georgina House opened its doors as an interdenominational women’s 
residence whose mission was “to provide houses and accommodation for girls and 
women earning their own livelihood where they could have all the benefits and comforts 
of home and be surrounded by a healthy moral influence until such time as they could 
be located in permanent places of abode which the Corporation would assist them to 
procure.”8 Room and board were available for $2.50 per week, with residents having 
access to communal living areas, events, and support. 
From the outset the organization appears to have had its eyes set on expansion; 
Georgina Cottage opened in the following years at 55 St. Patrick Street (now Dundas 
Street West), and in 1914 Spadina Lodge opened at 184 Spadina Avenue to provide 
shelter and support for unemployed and unhoused women. That same year saw the 
opening of the Osler Wing at 106 Beverley Street, a residential addition designed by 
Eden Smith & Son and officially opened by His Royal Highness the Duke of Connaught. 
By 1920, Georgina House was home to 20 long-term guests and had in the prior year 
accommodated 142 transients.9 In 1953, the neighbouring house at 108 Beverley Street 
was purchased and physically connected to Georgina House to provide additional 
accommodation and administrative spaces. 
Georgina House operated out of 106 Beverley Street through much of the 20th century, 
providing essential housing and a sense of community for countless women arriving in 
Toronto from across Canada and internationally, regardless of social, cultural, religious, 
and ethnic background. The organization was run by an all-woman board of 
management since 1917 and was able to respond to the needs and concerns of an 
exclusively female clientele during a period in which women were achieving economic 
autonomy and making significant gains in equality. Newspaper articles from this period

James Grand, Architect (1819-1871) 
The architect James Grand was born in England in 1819, however little biographical 
information has been recorded on his education or training. He immigrated to Toronto in 
the 1850s with the Royal Engineers and found employment with the architectural 
practice of Cumberland & Storm prior to establishing his own practice.11 Grand had an 
outsized influence on the growing city once he arrived; he is credited with the design of 
a handful of significant commissions including the Toronto Exchange Building (1854); 
the Ontario Veterinary College (1869); alterations to the Crystal Palace (1870); the 
Parliament, Bathurst, and York Street Schools (1871, with William G. Storm); and three 
fire halls (1871, with William Irving). He was the first architect in Toronto to utilize 
ferrovitreous construction, or glass and iron, which he employed to achieve a 40-foot 
interior domed room at the Toronto Exchange in 1854.12 
He was the father of James Grand (1857-1921), co-founder of the stationery firm Grand 
& Toy. James Grand passed away in Toronto in 1871, having demonstrated within just 
two decades of practice his adeptness in the design of a wide range of tastefully 
conservative buildings, of which a select few, including Georgina House, remain. 
John Jacques (1804-1886) 
Born in 1804 in England, John Jacques was a cabinetmaker, furniture manufacturer and 
in retirement, a financier who along with his business partner Robert Hay is credited 
with introducing high-quality, mass-produced and artistically distinct furniture to 
Southern Ontario through the mid to late-19th century. Jacques immigrated to York in 
1831 after apprenticing in England, likely at Wigton, Cumbria followed by London.13 In

York he found employment with William Maxwell, and in 1835 along with Robert Hay 
took over Maxwell’s business and renamed the firm to Jacques & Hay. The firm is 
credited not only with mass-producing quality furniture on a scale previously unseen in 
Upper Canada, but also with weaning the upper classes off American and European 
imports and establishing a regional Southern Ontario style. This style was typified by a 
sense of solidity, an absence of veneer, the use of black walnut as opposed to 
mahogany or oak, low ornamentation, and high gloss.14 
Jacques & Hay’s products were readily accessible to the growing middle-class market 
and thus the firm was able to capitalize on the growing anti-American sentiment and 
desire for uniquely Canadian products. They secured contracts to supply furnishings for 
significant institutions such as Osgoode Hall, along with the Sword’s Hotel, and James 
Austin’s Spadina House. After retiring in 1870 and moving to 106 Beverley Street the 
following year, Jacques utilized his wealth to continue to build his fortune, providing 
financing for banks, railways, and mortgages. Upon his passing in 1886 he left behind 
an estate of over $250,000.15 
Georgina Broughall (1843-1928) 
Harriet Georgina (Hurd) Broughall was born in Toronto in 1843 to Samuel Proudfoot 
Hurd, former Surveyor-General for Upper Canada, and Anne Mary Pratt. She married 
the Reverend Abraham James Broughall (1832-1917), who from 1861 until 1911 served 
as Rector for St Stephen-in-the-Fields Anglican Church (St. Stephen’s) at 103 Bellevue 
Avenue on the former Denison Estate. St. Stephen’s was founded by Robert Brittain 
Denison in 1857 to serve farmers on his estate (Bellevue House) and surrounding 
parishioners. During Broughall’s tenure the church was gutted by fire, re-built, expanded 
and renovated to serve the growing congregation, including an addition by Eden Smith, 
in 1890, who along with his son would go on to design a series of additions and 
alterations at Georgina House including unspecified interior alterations, the verandah 
(1909), a rear addition (1912), and Osler Wing (1914).16 
Georgina Broughall played an important and active role in the church as the rector’s 
wife and took a particular interest in the teaching of young women during bible class. It 
was through these lessons that she is purported to have recognized a need for secure 
housing for the increasing number of women arriving in Toronto seeking education and 
employment.17 Georgina petitioned support not only from St. Stephen’s, but from other 
Anglican Church parishes to which she was well-connected via sons who had pursued 
careers in the church, along with petitioning members of Toronto’s business community 
and the public at large via letter writing campaigns and publications. 
Georgina House opened in 1909, and Georgina Broughall continued to play an active 
role in the organization through its initial and rapid period of expansion leading up to 
World War I. Georgina Broughall stepped down from her position as President of

ii.  ARCHITECTURAL DESCRIPTION 
The following section provides an architectural description and analysis related to the 
property which will establish the basis for determining design or physical value of 
Criteria 1, 2 or 3 according to O. Reg. 9/06 Criteria. 
The subject property at 106 Beverley Street contains a three-storey detached house-
form building constructed in 1855 in the Italianate architectural style, and at the rear a 
1914 four-storey residential wing. The house is set-back from Beverley Street and is 
clad in brick that has been painted. The primary (east) façade features four bays of 
windows; the second storey windows set within elliptical openings while the third storey 
windows have rectangular heads. The second storey windows feature drip moulds with 
vermiculated key stones and sills (the material could not be confirmed). Brick quoins 
frame the second storey and support a simple brick string course that runs below the 
third storey windows. The roofline features a wooden cornice with simple brackets 
(larger brackets at the corners) and returns onto the north and south façades. The first 
storey is enclosed by a verandah which has itself been enclosed on the primary (east) 
façade, while remaining open on the southeast corner and return. The verandah 
features rectangular columns supporting a simple roof with cornice, wood railings, and 
spindles and a beamed ceiling. The enclosed portion of the verandah features large 
four-by-three paned windows. 
Behind the primary house-form building extends an “ell,” visible from Beverley Street, 
which is more restrained in ornamentation lacking the cornice, but retaining the brick 
quoins and window openings from the secondary (south) façade of the main house. At 
the rear and visible from Grange Place is the four-storey residential wing designed by 
Eden Smith & Son in 1914.18 The rectangular wing is clad in unpainted brick with 
minimal ornamentation; the west façade features four bays of rectangular windows with 
two-over-two hung sashes, what appear to be steel lintels, and stone sills. 
The Italianate architectural style was a popular, classically derived architectural style in 
the mid-19th century for both residential and commercial buildings across the British 
colonies and the United States. The style was inspired by the architecture of 
Renaissance Italy and was an alternative to the more stoic Classical and Gothic Revival 
architectural styles. Key features of the Italianate style include flat or low-hipped roofs; 
tall and narrow arched or elliptical window openings; quoins; large cornices with dentils 
and brackets; and cladding in stone, stucco, and brick.

iii. CONTEXT 
The following section provides contextual information and analysis related to the 
property which is the basis for determining contextual value of Criteria 7, 8 or 9 
according to O. Reg. 9/06 Criteria. 
The City of Toronto Property Data Map attached (Attachment 2) shows the site of the 
property at 106 Beverley Street. 
The subject property at 106 Beverley Street is located on the west side of Beverley 
Street south of Dundas Street West within the Grange neighbourhood of downtown 
Toronto. To the north are three pairs of two-storey semi-detached Edwardian-era 
house-form buildings; to the south are two two-storey Edwardian apartments. Directly 
across from the subject property is the Art Gallery of Ontario, comprising the Georgian 
manor which gave the area its name, built in 1817 for D’Arcy Boulton, and onto which 
later additions have been constructed. Grange Park, formerly St. George’s Square, 
extends to the south of the manor house, terminating at the grounds of St. George’s 
Anglican Church and the clock tower that remains following a fire in 1955. 
The Grange neighbourhood is a primarily residential district of Victorian- and 
Edwardian-era houses, interspersed with places of worship and institutional buildings. 
Within this context Beverley Street and those streets immediately adjacent contain the 
area’s largest and most prestigious houses, including Boulton’s Grange (317 Dundas 
Street West, 1817); George Beardmore’s Chudleigh (136 Beverley Street, 1890); John 
Cawthra’s Devon House (150 Beverley Street, 1875); and George Brown’s Lambton 
Lodge (50 Baldwin Street and 186 Beverley Street, 1876). Georgina House at 106 
Beverley Street fits within this context of mid- to late-Victorian era houses within the 
Grange neighbourhood and reflects this important period of development in Toronto.
